newsitem.title: UK: IRA bomb suspects face extradition to Germany.
newsitem.headline: IRA bomb suspects face extradition to Germany.

text.p: Two people from Northern Ireland wanted by Germany in connection with an IRA mortar bomb attack on a British army base were sent to prison in London and Dublin on Wednesday to await extradition hearings.

Roisin McAliskey, daughter of former nationalist member of parliament Bernadette McAliskey, a prominent republican in the 1960s as Bernadette Devlin, was remanded in custody for one week by a London court after being arrested in Northern Ireland last week.

The second suspect, 28-year-old James Corry, was arrested in the centre of Dublin on Wednesday on a provisional extradition request from Germany. He was also remanded in custody for one week after a 15-minute hearing in the Irish capital.
Both are suspected of involvement in the attack on the army base near the northwest German town of Osnabrueck last June.
McAliskey, 25, spoke only to confirm her name, date of birth and that she understood the charges. She was remanded in custody for one week and will be held at London's Holloway prison.
"She is innocent of the offences of which she is charged," Gareth Pierce, McAliskey's soliticor, told magistrates at Bow Street court.

"They (German authorities) are charging she was a member of a provisional IRA active service unit responsible for the mortar attack on the British barracks," John Pierre Le Tissier, a British police detective, told the court.
Pierce told the court McAliskey was four and a half months pregnant, "represented no threat to the public", and should be released on bail after the next hearing, due to take place on December 4.

"There are complications with this pregnancy," Pierce said. "The doctor who saw her last night (Tuesday) said it was imperative she not go anywhere that does not have specialist obstetrics facilities."
The June 26 attack was one of the IRA's least successful in its fight to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Only one of three mortar bombs fired at the barracks exploded and that fell several yards (metres) short of its target, a diesel pump for military vehicles. No one was injured.
The Osnabrueck attack was the first in mainland Europe following the end of the IRA's 17-month ceasefire in February.
The guerrilla group has set off a series of bombs in Britain. It also staged a car bombing at the British army's headquarters in Northern Ireland in which one soldier was killed.
